Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Shigella infections are rising in the U.S., with 8.5% of samples in 2023 resistant to standard antibiotics, including azithromycin and ciprofloxacin. These bacteria cause severe, contagious diarrhea (shigellosis) and are particularly risky for children and immunocompromised adults. No FDA-approved oral treatment currently exists for these strains. Key Details on Drug-Resistant Shigella Definition: XDR Shigella is resistant to all standard antibiotic treatments: ampicillin, azithromycin, ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX). Rising Threat: Cases have grown substantially since 2016, with 12% of California cases being XDR as of May 2024, representing a 78% increase from 2023. Symptoms: Intense diarrhea (often bloody), fever, and stomach pain. High-Risk Groups: While anyone can be infected, cases are high among adult men, particularly gay or bisexual men, international travelers, and people with compromised immune systems. Transmission: Spread easily through fecal-oral contact (contaminated food, water, or surfaces). Treatment and Prevention Limited Options: Because standard antibiotics often fail, doctors may need to manage symptoms with fluids, as most infections resolve on their own in about a week. Prevention: Thorough handwashing with soap and water is crucial. Precautions: Avoid swimming in pools, lakes, or ponds when infected or for several days after diarrhea stops. For more information, visit the CDC's page on antimicrobial-resistant Shigella. CDC's page on antimicrobial-resistant Shigella
